title: Taming the Hippo Defense | Develop Your Instincts | GM Naroditsky's DYI Speedrun

moves.spoken: The point I keep coming back to is never to fall in love with a particular piece. One more game — we face a fianchetto, e4 and g6.
We stake out the center with d4.

Black tries d5 — not a move that's typically studied or theoretical. It's not terrible, but Black falls behind in development and in space, and there are two ways to meet it: push e5 for a big center, or capture.
We take, e takes d5, opening the position while Black is underdeveloped.
Black recaptures with the queen on d5, pulling the queen out early — always risky.
Now just follow basic principles: the knight to c3, exactly like the Scandinavian, developing with tempo against the queen.
Black digs a deeper hole with the queen to e6 with check — a really bad move: it blocks in the bishop and stumbles the queen into the crossfire.
I block the check with the bishop to e3. Several moves are roughly equal here, but I have a specific plan in mind that I'll detail after the game.
Black fianchettoes with the bishop to g7. Meanwhile I'm already picturing where I want to castle — queenside — and where the attack goes: the kingside.
The queen comes to d2, connecting the plan: it eyes the h6-square and prepares to castle long.
Black develops the knight to f6.
I follow through on the concept and castle queenside, anticipating that Black castles kingside — opposite-side castling means a pawn-storm race.
Black castles kingside, right into the teeth of where I want to attack.
I take the middle ground and develop the knight to f3 before committing the h-pawn.
Black plays b6, preparing to fianchetto the other bishop.
One option is the bishop to h6, offering the trade of dark-squared bishops; another is h4, though h4 often meets h5 and stalls.
Black continues the fianchetto with the bishop to b7.
You don't automatically have to take on g7 in these positions, but here I will — the bishop takes on g7.
Black recaptures with the king on g7, and now those dark squares around his king are permanently tender.
A note for newer players: instead of trading, you can keep the tension and drive the pawn up to h5, which can be much more effective because it keeps Black's h-pawn a prisoner.
But taking is clean too — the bishops come off, which guarantees Black lasting problems on the dark squares around his king.
The knight leaps to e5. We don't have to restrict ourselves to the kingside; we can play in the center and against Black's queen — exactly what I'm doing.
Black develops the knight to a6 — no reason not to bring it out toward c5.
I complete development with the bishop to c4, and now Black's queen doesn't have many good squares.
I'm anticipating the queen to d6 — probably the only reasonable retreat for Black.
I play the quiet f3. Where is the attack headed? To the b-file eventually — and I'm also watching that the knight to b5 could, under the right circumstances, trap the queen.
Black plays c6, taking the b5-square away from my knight.
Now h4 — this is the moment in every attack where you press the gas pedal down.
Black grabs space of his own with b5.
h5 — when the attack is overwhelming enough you start sacrificing without agonizing over every line.
Black takes, the knight capturing on h5.
Recapturing on h5 with the rook is playable but not most accurate — I think g4 is far more straightforward, keeping our rook for bigger things while trapping the knight.
The knight scurries back to f6.
The queen swings to h6 with check — Black is making it very easy for us.
Black tucks the king to g8.
Now the final, important step: we need to deflect that f6-knight, and the most clinical way is with another knight — the knight to e4.
There are other winning moves here too — the knight takes on g6, or g5, though g5 is less clean because of the knight to h5 in reply.
But the knight to e4 is the surgical choice, hitting the defending knight and clearing the path to the king.
Black tries the rook to d8, seeking counterplay on the d-file.
My mouse slipped to the queen on f4, but it doesn't change anything — I'm still totally winning.
I'd intended a mate in two of course — the bishop to f7 and the knight to g6 — but no worries, the position is overwhelming.
After the queen to f4, Black takes the bishop with b takes c4, and we simply grab the queen — the knight takes on d6.
Black recaptures the knight with the rook on d6, and we push g5, chasing the last defender.
Black lunges with the knight to b4, and we crash through, g takes f6, peeling the cover off the king.
Black grabs the pawn with the rook on f6, and the queen returns to h6, back on the attack.
Black flails with the knight taking on a2 with check, trying to flag me on the clock.
We calmly step the king to b1.
Black continues the desperado, the knight to c3 with check.
We take, b takes c3 — a noble but hopeless try.
If Black plays e6, ask yourself: what's the fastest checkmate here? A lot of players automatically grab the pawn and let the king wriggle out.
Your instinct should be to seal off the escape route — the knight to d7, not a check. Cutting off the flight square beats a flashy check.
Black blocks with the bishop to c8, and the queen takes on h7 — checkmate.
Let me start from the end and show you a classic Karpov-Korchnoi game — one of their earlier meetings, with Karpov about twenty-one — that illustrates this exact deflection theme.
I like to give real context when we run into a recurring theme, so bear with the little tactical lecture.
Rewinding into the attack again to trace the pattern from the top.
A sample continuation: the rook to e8, the knight to c3, the rook back to f8, and the queen to h6 — the mating net keeps reforming no matter how Black shuffles.
In my own game it was very simple — you just go the knight to e4 and the attack breaks through.
As for the opening there isn't much to discuss; the one thing to note is how I handled the bishop.
After the queen check, the bishop to e3 blocks and sets up the quick castle queenside.
Black fianchettoes, and the queen to d2 keeps the long-castling plan on rails.
Black develops the knight, and we castle queenside.
Black castles kingside, and we bring the knight to f3.
Black plays b6 — and here's the second big theme: I combine play on the kingside with play in the center.
Some of you were worried about the bishop to h6.
If Black trades on h6 and then jumps the knight to g4 hitting the queen, this is rarely a problem — you can drop the queen back to d2, but there's a better move.
The queen to h4 is stronger, threatening to win outright with the knight to g5.
The knight to h6, the queen to g5, the knight back to g4, the queen to h6 — this dance usually doesn't cost any material at all.
Back to the main position after the fianchetto.
We take on g7 and Black recaptures with the king, then we stick the knight into the center.
The knight to e5, a beautiful central outpost.
Black plays the knight to a6, and we develop the bishop to c4.
Black's queen comes to d6.
And one slow move — f3 — can really make the position breathe.
Notice we weren't afraid of the knight to b4.
Because the knight to b5 hits back with an x-ray, and the c6-push turns out meaningless.
So after c6, the knight to c3, the knight to a6, we crash through with h4 — h5 straight away would have been met by g4.
Black plays h5 and we answer g4.
Black takes, h takes g4.
And h5 — this is the very typical attacking method: throw away all your pawns to rip open the files.

We'll get plenty more chances to do this kind of thing, so I won't go too deep — but remember, you don't always need to attack by sacrificing, especially when your opponent isn't creating any counter-threats.
The knight to c3, b5, h4, the knight to a6 — the same storming structure, ready to break through.
